claims.text: The proposed intervention is solution annealing HfZrTiTa0.53 at approximately 1200 K for about 1 hour followed by aging at approximately 800 K for about 2 hours.
The specified two-step heat treatment will produce a partially recrystallized microstructure.
The specified two-step heat treatment will produce finely dispersed nanoscale Ta-enriched precipitates.
Subsequent thermomechanical treatment can control precipitate size, morphology, and distribution and thereby optimize strength and ductility in multicomponent alloys.
The treatment will refine grains and improve grain-boundary quality in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Refined grains and dispersed precipitates will enhance dislocation storage and provide back-stress strengthening.
Enhanced dislocation storage and back-stress strengthening will delay necking and promote more uniform tensile plastic deformation.
The microstructural changes will not degrade energetic fragmentation behavior.
The initial HfZrTiTa0.53 is single-phase or nominally homogeneous.
As-cast or similarly processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
As-cast or similarly processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
As-cast or similarly processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a terminal compressive strain of 13.5%.
The heat treatment will increase room-temperature uniform tensile elongation by at least 30% relative to the stated 13.5% baseline.
The heat treatment will limit the decrease in yield strength to no more than approximately 5% relative to 786 MPa.
The heat-treated material will retain comparable or improved impact-induced energy release.
The hypothesis applies to tensile loading from room temperature to approximately 700 K at strain rates of 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1.
At 673 K and a strain rate of 1×10^-3 s^-1, a different refractory alloy, NbTaTiZrV0.5, showed reduced strength and greatly increased plasticity.
Successful ductility and impact-energy retention depend on forming uniform fine precipitates rather than coarse embrittling phases.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% value is identified as terminal strain measured under compression, but it is subsequently used as the baseline for a claimed 30% increase in uniform tensile elongation. Terminal compressive strain and uniform tensile elongation are different loading-mode-dependent metrics and cannot serve as the same baseline without a separate tensile measurement.
